Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio test for nested mixture models

Source: R/enumeration.R
bootstrap_lrt.Rd

The parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio test evaluates whether a more flexible mixture model provides an improvement in fit that is inconsistent with a simpler, nested model. bootstrap_lrt() compares two fitted models using twice the difference between their maximized log likelihoods. In class enumeration, this comparison assesses the evidence for adding a latent profile or group class.

The function generates datasets from the fitted null model and refits both candidate models to each dataset. These simulated comparisons approximate the distribution of the likelihood-ratio statistic under the null hypothesis. The observed statistic is then evaluated against this distribution to obtain a bootstrap p-value. This approach avoids relying on the usual chi-squared approximation, which is generally inappropriate when comparing different numbers of mixture components.

The result includes the observed test statistic, bootstrap p-value, Monte Carlo standard error, and diagnostics for the simulated refits. The function supports profile and class models, latent transition models, and group-class model families, subject to the nesting and compatibility requirements below.

Usage

bootstrap_lrt(
  null_model,
  alternative_model,
  data = NULL,
  iter = 199L,
  n_starts = NULL,
  max_iter = NULL,
  tol = NULL,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

null_model

A converged fitted model representing the null hypothesis. Supported inputs are profile or class models, with or without membership covariates; transition models from lta(); and group-class models fitted through multilpa(). See Supported comparisons for nesting requirements.

alternative_model

A compatible, more flexible model fitted to the same data, within which null_model is nested.

data

The data frame used to fit both models. Required for transition models, whose simulations retain the observed groups, occasions and covariates. For ordinary profile and class models, omission reconstructs the data from the null fit, or from the alternative for membership-covariate models. For group-class models, the stored sufficient statistics are used when data is omitted. Supplied data are checked against the fitted models.

iter

Number of simulated datasets; default 199. Profile, class and group-class comparisons require at least two replicates; transition comparisons accept any positive integer. Larger values reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty in the estimated p-value.

n_starts

Number of starts for each simulated fit. With NULL (the default), each model retains its original number of starts and search strategy. A supplied number applies to both models.

max_iter

Maximum iterations for each simulated fit. With NULL (the default), each model retains its original iteration limit.

tol

Convergence tolerance for each simulated fit. With NULL (the default), each model retains its original tolerance.

seed

Optional integer seed accepted by set.seed(). The caller's random-number state is restored on exit.

Value

An object of class multilpa_bootstrap_lrt containing the observed statistic, bootstrap p-value, Monte Carlo standard error, numbers of valid and invalid replicates, and replicate-level diagnostics. The fixed component identifies any measurement blocks held constant.

as.data.frame() returns a one-row test summary. get_results(result, what = "replicates") returns one row per simulated replicate. summary() combines the test summary and replicate diagnostics; plot() displays the simulated reference distribution and observed statistic.

Interpretation

A small p-value provides evidence against the null model in favour of the specified alternative, subject to the model assumptions and the quality of estimation. It does not establish that the alternative has the correct number of classes or fits the data adequately in an absolute sense. Interpretation should consider convergence, replication across starting values, and the frequency of invalid bootstrap replicates. Increasing the number of replicates reduces simulation uncertainty but does not resolve systematic estimation problems.

Supported comparisons

For ordinary profile and class models, with or without membership covariates, the models must differ by exactly one observation-level profile or class, or by exactly one group class. They must use the same observations, group layout, covariance structure, centering and scaling, missing-data handling, and drop_empty setting. Grand-mean centering is repeated in each simulated refit. Person-centred or person-scaled fits are not supported, because the model does not specify a distribution for the group baselines removed by these transformations.

Transition models fitted with lta() support comparisons in which the null specification is nested within the alternative. Supported differences include class counts and restrictions on measurement, transition probabilities, Markov order, and covariate effects. Both models must use compatible indicators, grouping, occasion layout, and measurement distributions. The original data must be supplied for transition comparisons.

Group-class models fitted through the family argument of multilpa() support comparisons across class counts and parameter restrictions. The null must be nested within, and distinct from, the alternative: the alternative must have at least as many group classes and cannot impose additional restrictions on the class-specific means or variance components. Models from different families cannot be combined arbitrarily.

For membership-covariate models, covariates are held at their observed values when simulating data. Group classes and profiles are drawn using the fitted membership probabilities. Both models must use the same profile covariates, group covariates and slope specification, except that a one-group-class null may be compared with an alternative that adds group covariates or slopes that vary by group class.

For models fitted with fixed, including those from fit_staged(), each replicate retains the same fixed blocks at the same values. The resulting p-value is conditional on that measurement solution; uncertainty in its estimation is not propagated. Pairs for which nesting cannot be established are rejected.

Bootstrap calculation

The observed statistic is 2 * (logLik(alternative_model) - logLik(null_model)). Datasets are simulated under the fitted null model, retaining the group structure and other design features required by the model family. Both models are refitted to each simulated dataset and the statistic is recalculated. By default, each model retains its original search controls; n_starts, max_iter and tol can override the corresponding settings for both models.

The bootstrap p-value is (1 + b) / (V + 1), where b is the number of valid simulated statistics at least as large as the observed statistic and V is the number of valid replicates. When all replicates are valid, V = iter. The reported Monte Carlo standard error summarizes uncertainty from the finite number of simulated replicates.

Estimation failures

Both original models must have converged. A simulated replicate is invalid if a refit fails, does not converge, or produces an alternative-model likelihood below the null-model likelihood beyond numerical tolerance. The result reports n_valid and n_invalid; latents_failed_replicates warns when any replicate is invalid. The p-value uses only valid replicates and is NA when fewer than half of the requested replicates are valid.

Excluding invalid replicates conditions the reference distribution on successful estimation and may affect calibration. Report the invalid proportion and examine the replicate diagnostics before interpreting the test.

For membership-covariate models, a simulated refit is considered converged for this test when its likelihood has converged, even if a membership logit is still changing. This can occur with an empty or separated class in an alternative model. The logits_settled column records whether the logits also converged. The original covariate models must be fully converged.

Missing-data assumptions

Fits estimated with missing = "fiml" are supported when both models use that setting. Each simulated dataset retains the original missing-value pattern before refitting. Calibration requires missingness independent of the indicators and latent classes, conditional on any fixed covariates. A fixed missingness pattern does not reproduce a missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism that depends on observed indicators or a missing-not-at-random (MNAR) mechanism. Valid FIML estimation under MAR does not by itself establish validity of this bootstrap under MAR.

Conditions

For ordinary profile and class comparisons, latents_bad_nesting indicates incompatible class counts, fixed measurement blocks, covariate specifications, or parameter counts. latents_incomparable_models indicates incompatible data or fitting specifications. Transition and group-class comparisons use their family-specific nesting checks and raise latents_bad_argument for unsupported nesting requests. Transition models also raise latents_bad_argument when data is omitted.

latents_unsupported_bootstrap identifies unsupported person centering or scaling. Models with a prior, sampling weights or a noise component raise latents_unsupported_prior, latents_unsupported_weights or latents_unsupported_noise, respectively. latents_bad_data identifies unsupported missing indicators, and latents_bad_inference_data identifies supplied data that do not reproduce the original fitting data or likelihood.

latents_no_converge indicates that an original model has not converged; for ordinary profile and class models it also identifies active variance bounds. latents_reversed_likelihood indicates that the alternative has a lower likelihood than the null beyond numerical tolerance. Invalid seeds or incompatible model families raise latents_bad_argument. latents_failed_replicates warns about invalid simulated replicates; see Estimation failures for their treatment.

References

Nylund, K. L., Asparouhov, T., & Muthen, B. O. (2007). Deciding on the number of classes in latent class analysis and growth mixture modeling: A Monte Carlo simulation study. Structural Equation Modeling, 14(4), 535–569.

See also

enumerate_classes() for fitting candidate models; compare_models() for information-criterion comparisons.

Examples

set.seed(1)
example_data <- data.frame(
  school = rep(seq_len(10), each = 10),
  score = rnorm(100, rep(c(-2, 2), each = 50))
)
smaller <- multilpa(example_data, "score", "school", n_profiles = 1,
                    n_group_classes = 1, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
larger <- multilpa(example_data, "score", "school", n_profiles = 2,
                   n_group_classes = 1, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
# `iter` is small so the example runs quickly; use many more for inference.
comparison <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, iter = 9, n_starts = 1,
                            max_iter = 2000, tol = 1e-6, seed = 1)
comparison
#> Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison
#> Null: 1 profile; alternative: 2 profiles
#> Observed statistic: 44.198110
#> p-value: 0.1 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0949) from 9 of 9 valid replicates (0 invalid)
